themes.title: Harappan civilisation, early urbanism & civilisational continuity
themes.asks: UPSC asks about Harappan architecture and town planning, and pushes you to connect it to today: lessons for modern urbanisation, and why Indian civilisation survived without a break unlike Egypt or Mesopotamia. Geography's role in shaping ancient India also comes up.
checklist: Harappan town planning: grid layout, drainage, citadel vs lower town, granaries, Great Bath, burnt bricks
Lessons for present cities: drainage, water harvesting (Dholavira), zoning
Continuity of Indian civilisation: language, religion, crafts, agriculture practices that survived
Comparison points with Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece
Geography of ancient India: rivers, monsoon, Himalayan barrier, passes, coastline
answer: Use one or two named sites (Dholavira, Lothal, Mohenjo-daro) as evidence in every answer
For 'present-day relevance' questions, split the body into then vs now and end with a takeaway for smart cities

questions.text: Discuss the salient features of the Harappan architecture.
Explain the role of geographical factors towards the development of Ancient India.

The ancient civilization in Indian sub-continent differed from those of Egypt, Mesopotamia and Greece in that its culture and traditions have been preserved without a breakdown to the present day. Comment.
To what extent has the urban planning and culture of the Indus Valley Civilization provided inputs to the present day urbanization? Discuss.

themes.title: Vedic society & its legacy in today's society
themes.asks: Questions trace change from Rig Vedic to Later Vedic society and economy, and ask which Vedic features still live on in Indian society.
checklist: Rig Vedic vs Later Vedic: pastoral to agrarian, tribe to territorial state, varna hardening, position of women
Vedic religion: nature gods, yajna, rise of ritualism and Upanishadic reaction
Surviving features: rituals, varna/caste, gotra, sanskaras, family structure
answer: A two-column comparison (Rig vs Later Vedic) works well in 150 words
For 'still prevailing' questions, give the feature, then a present example, then how it has changed

questions.text: Underline the changes in the field of society and economy from the Rig Vedic to the later Vedic period.
What are the main features of Vedic society and religion? Do you think some of the features are still prevailing in Indian society?

themes.title: Sources of history: inscriptions, rock-cut caves, travellers, Sangam & Persian texts
themes.asks: UPSC asks how specific sources help reconstruct history: Ashokan inscriptions, rock-cut caves, Chinese and Arab travellers, Persian texts, Sangam literature. The angle is always 'what does this source tell us, and what are its limits'.
checklist: Ashokan edicts: dhamma, administration, extent of empire, script (Brahmi, Kharosthi)
Rock-cut caves: Barabar, Ajanta, Ellora, Elephanta and what they reveal on art, religion, patronage
Travellers: Megasthenes, Fa-Hien, Hiuen Tsang, Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta
Persian sources: Ain-i-Akbari, Baburnama, court chronicles
Sangam literature: social and economic life vs weak political chronology
answer: Structure: what the source is → what it reveals (polity, economy, society, religion) → its limitations or biases
Name at least three specific examples per answer

questions.text: Analyze the importance of Ashokan inscriptions for reconstructing Mauryan history
The rock-cut architecture represents one of the most important sources of our knowledge of early Indian art and history. Discuss.
Persian literary sources of medieval India reflect the spirit of the age. Comment.
Assess the importance of the accounts of the Chinese and Arab travellers in the reconstruction of the history of India.

Though not very useful from the point of view of a connected political history of South India, the Sangam literature portrays the social and economic conditions of its time with remarkable vividness. Comment.

themes.title: Buddhist art & sculpture schools: stupa, Gandhara, Pala
themes.asks: Questions focus on how Buddhist art expressed ideas: stupa reliefs using folk motifs, Gandhara's Greek and Roman influences, and the Pala period's importance for Buddhism.
checklist: Stupa art: Sanchi, Bharhut, Amaravati, jataka narratives, aniconic phase
Gandhara vs Mathura vs Amaravati schools: material, features, influences
Pala period: Nalanda, Vikramashila, Vajrayana, art and spread to Tibet and South-East Asia
answer: Compare schools in a short table if the question allows
Always link the art feature to the Buddhist idea it carries

questions.text: Pala period is the most significant phase in the history of Buddhism in India. Enumerate.
Early Buddhist Stupa-art, while depicting folk motifs and narratives successfully expounds Buddhist ideals. Elucidate.
Gandhara sculpture owed as much to the Romans as to the Greeks. Explain.

themes.title: Temple architecture & regional dynasties: Pallava, Chola, Chandela, Vijayanagara, Gupta
themes.asks: The most repeated culture area. UPSC asks about specific dynasties (Pallava, Chola, Chandela, Vijayanagara, Gupta) and their contribution to art and architecture, and how philosophy shaped monuments.
checklist: Nagara, Dravida and Vesara styles: key features and examples
Pallavas: Mamallapuram rathas, Shore Temple, Kailasanatha; also literature
Vijayanagara: Hampi, blending older Dravida tradition with new features
Gupta contributions: temples, sculpture, literature, science
How Indian philosophy (cosmology, iconography, vastu) shaped monuments
answer: Open with the dynasty's period and region, then architecture, sculpture, literature/other arts
Name temples and specific features — examiners reward precise examples
Quote-based questions ('…still remembered with pride') need you to justify the quote with evidence

questions.text: Vijayanagara architecture exemplifies the amalgamation of past traditions with contemporary practices. Elucidate with examples
'The sculptors filled the Chandella artform with resilient vigor and breadth of life.' Elucidate.
Estimate the contribution of Pallavas of Kanchi for the development of art and literature of South India.
"Though the great Cholas are no more yet their name is still remembered with great pride because of their highest achievements in the domain of art and architecture." Comment.
Discuss the main contributions of Gupta period and Chola period to Indian Heritage and Culture.
Indian philosophy and tradition played a significant role in conceiving and shaping the monuments and their art in India. Discuss.
(a) Discuss the ‘Tandava’ dance as recorded in early Indian inscriptions. (b) Chola architecture represents a high watermark in the evolution of temple architecture. Discuss.

themes.title: Sculpture, painting, motifs, coins & safeguarding art heritage
themes.asks: Questions ask what sculpture and painting reveal (temple sculpture as a record of social life, Mesolithic rock art), the meaning of motifs (lion and bull), Gupta coins, and the need to safeguard art heritage.
checklist: Medieval temple sculpture as social record: dance, music, war, daily life
Lion and bull motifs: Harappan seals, Mauryan capitals, mythology
Mesolithic rock art: Bhimbetka, themes, technique
Gupta numismatics: gold coins, themes, decline later
Heritage protection: ASI, laws, illegal trade, repatriation, UNESCO
answer: Use 'evidence → interpretation' format
For heritage protection, end with concrete measures (digitisation, community role, laws)

questions.text: How will you explain that medieval Indian temple sculptures represent the social life of those days?
Discuss the significance of the lion and Bull figures in Indian Mythology art and architecture.
Safeguarding the Indian art heritage is the need of the moment. Discuss.
How do you justify the view that the level of excellence of the Gupta numismatic art is not at all noticeable in later times?
Mesolithic rock cut architecture of India not only reflects the cultural life of the times but also a fine aesthetic sense comparable to modern painting. Critically evaluate this comment.

themes.title: Bhakti–Sufi movements & religious syncretism
themes.asks: UPSC asks about the nature and contribution of Bhakti literature, Chaitanya's role, whether Sufis and saints really changed society, and Akbar's syncretism.
checklist: Bhakti: Alvars and Nayanars, Kabir, Nanak, Mirabai, Chaitanya; saguna vs nirguna
Contribution: regional languages, social equality message, music
Sufism: silsilas (Chishti, Suhrawardi), khanqah, interaction with bhakti
Limits: caste and religious structures largely remained
Akbar: sulh-i-kul, Ibadat Khana, Din-i-Ilahi, translation bureau
answer: For 'failed to modify' type statements, give both sides: changes in ideas and language vs continuity in structures
Link to Indian secularism where relevant

questions.text: Examine the main aspects of Akbar's religious syncretism.
Evaluate the nature of Bhakti Literature and its contribution to Indian culture.
The Bhakti movement received a remarkable re-orientation with the advent of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Discuss.
Sufis and medieval mystic saints failed to modify either the religious ideas and practices or the outward structure of Hindu / Muslim societies to any appreciable extent. Comment.

themes.title: Patronage, learning centres & medieval technology
themes.asks: Questions ask about royal patronage of learning (Krishnadeva Raya), ancient universities (Taxila vs Nalanda), and technology introduced in the Sultanate period.
checklist: Krishnadeva Raya: Amuktamalyada, Ashtadiggajas, Telugu and Sanskrit literature
Taxila vs Nalanda: subjects, scholars, why Nalanda fits the 'university' idea
Sultanate technology: paper, spinning wheel, arch and dome, Persian wheel, and their social effects
answer: Link each technology to the social change it caused
For Taxila, explain why it was a centre of learning rather than an organised university

questions.text: What were the major technological changes introduced during the Sultanate period? How did those technological changes influence the Indian society?
Krishnadeva Raya, the King of Vijayanagar, was not only an accomplished scholar himself but was also a great patron of learning and literature. Discuss.

Taxila university was one of the oldest universities of the world with which were associated a number of renowned learned personalities of different disciplines. Its strategic location caused its fame to flourish, but unlike Nalanda, it is not considered as a university in the modern sense. Discuss.

themes.title: British expansion: fragmented polity, Panipat, why the Company won, Dalhousie
themes.asks: UPSC asks why the East India Company won against larger Indian armies, how 18th-century India was politically fragmented, why Panipat saw repeated battles, and Dalhousie's role.
checklist: Decline of Mughals and rise of regional states
Plassey, Buxar, Anglo-Mysore, Anglo-Maratha, Anglo-Sikh wars
Reasons for British success: discipline, finance, diplomacy, divisions among rulers
Dalhousie: doctrine of lapse, railways, telegraph, postal reforms
answer: Group reasons into military, economic, political and organisational
Use specific battles as evidence

questions.text: Why did the armies of the British East India company – mostly comprising of Indian soldiers – win consistently against the more numerous and better equipped armies of then Indian rulers? Give reasons.
Clarify how mid-eighteenth century India was beset with the spectre of a fragmented polity?
The third battle of Panipat was fought in 1761. Why were so many empire-shaking battles fought at Panipat?
“In many ways, Lord Dalhousie was the founder of modern India.” Elaborate.

themes.title: Colonial economy: drain, deindustrialisation, famines, economic policy
themes.asks: Questions repeat on how British policies hurt India's economy: decline of handicrafts, collapse of the rural artisan economy, famines, and an overall critical assessment of British economic policy.
checklist: Drain of wealth (Naoroji), land revenue systems (Permanent, Ryotwari, Mahalwari)
Deindustrialisation: competition from British machine goods, loss of royal patronage
Famines: commercialisation of agriculture, revenue demands, policy failures
Railways and commercialisation: who gained, who lost
answer: Structure by phases (mercantile, free trade, finance capital) for 'mid-18th century till independence' questions
Always link back to the rural economy and peasants

questions.text: How far was the Industrial Revolution in England responsible for the decline of handicrafts and cottage industries in India?
Why was there a sudden spurt in famines in colonial India since the mid-18th century? Give reasons.
Examine how the decline of traditional artisanal industry in colonial India crippled the rural economy.
Examine critically the various facets of economic policies of the British in India from mid-eighteenth century till independence.

themes.title: Colonial administration & education policy: Macaulay, Curzon
themes.asks: UPSC asks about policies that shaped administration and education (Macaulay's Minute) and Curzon's policies and their long-term effect on the national movement.
checklist: Effects: English-educated class staffing administration, and the same class leading nationalism
Curzon: partition of Bengal, Universities Act 1904, Calcutta Corporation Act, Indian Official Secrets Act
Curzon's policies triggering Swadeshi and extremism
answer: Show intended aims and unintended effects (education producing nationalists)

questions.text: Discuss the impact of Macaulay’s Minute on colonial administration and education in India
Evaluate the policies of Lord Curzon and their long term implications on the national movement.

themes.title: 1857 and tribal–peasant resistance to colonial rule
themes.asks: Questions ask how 1857 changed British policy and how colonial rule affected tribals and how they resisted.
checklist: 1857: causes, spread, nature, consequences, Queen's Proclamation, army reorganisation, policy towards princes
Colonial impact on tribals: forest laws, land alienation, moneylenders, missionaries
Tribal revolts: Santhal, Munda (Birsa), Bhil, Rampa
answer: Name specific movements and leaders
Tribal questions benefit from a link to present-day tribal policy and forest rights

questions.text: How did the colonial rule affect the tribals in India and what was the tribal response to the colonial oppression?
Explain how the upraising of 1857 constitutes an important watershed in the evolution of British policies towards colonial India.

themes.title: Socio-religious reform: Brahmo Samaj, Young Bengal, Phule
themes.asks: UPSC asks about the rise of reform movements (Brahmo Samaj, Young Bengal) and reformers like Phule who addressed subaltern groups.
checklist: Brahmo Samaj, Young Bengal, Prarthana Samaj, Arya Samaj, Ramakrishna Mission
Phule: Satyashodhak Samaj, Gulamgiri, education for women and lower castes
Caste reformers: Narayana Guru, Periyar, Ambedkar
answer: Organise by region or by issue (caste, women, religion)
Link reformers' ideas to constitutional values today

questions.text: Mahatma Jotirao Phule's writings and efforts of social reforms touched issues of almost all subaltern classes. Discuss.
Trace the rise and growth of socio-religious reform movements with special reference to Young Bengal and Brahmo Samaj.

themes.title: Early nationalism: Moderates & foreign contributors
themes.asks: Questions assess the Moderates: did they lay the base for the freedom movement, and why did they fail to convince the nation? Foreigners' contribution also appears.
checklist: Moderates: petitions, economic critique of British rule, drain theory, building public opinion
Limitations: narrow social base, faith in British justice
Foreigners: Annie Besant, Sister Nivedita, A.O. Hume, C.F. Andrews, Madeleine Slade
answer: Balance achievements and limitations
Use names and specific contributions

questions.text: To what extent did the role of the moderates prepare a base for the wider freedom movement? Comment.
Why did the ‘Moderates’ fail to carry conviction with the nation about their proclaimed ideology and political goals by the end of the nineteenth century?
Several foreigners made India their homeland and participated in various movements. Analyze their role in the Indian struggle for freedom.

themes.title: Gandhi: mass movements, constructive programme, ideas & contemporaries
themes.asks: Gandhi is UPSC's favourite personality: mass mobilisation, constructive programmes, his relevance today, comparison with Tagore, Ambedkar and Bose, and whether independence would differ without him.
checklist: Gandhian movements: Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad, Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India — who was mobilised
Constructive programme: khadi, Hindu-Muslim unity, untouchability removal, basic education
Gandhi vs Tagore (education, nationalism), vs Ambedkar (caste, strategy), vs Bose (methods)
Relevance today: non-violence, sustainable living, decentralisation, conflict resolution
answer: For comparisons, a clear 'common goal, different method' frame scores well
For 'relevance today', link each Gandhian idea to a current issue

questions.text: The significance of the Gandhian movements lay in the masses they mobilized. Elucidate
What was the difference between Mahatma Gandhi and Rabindranath Tagore in their approach towards education and nationalism?
Bring out the constructive programmes of Mahatma Gandhi during Non-Cooperation Movement and Civil Disobedience Movement.
Throw light on the significance of thoughts of Mahatma Gandhi in the present times.
Highlight the difference in the approach of Subhash Chandra Bose and Mahatma Gandhi in the struggle for freedom.
How different would have been the achievement of Indian independence without Mahatma Gandhi? Discuss.
Mahatma Gandhi and Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, despite having divergent approaches and strategies, had a common goal of amelioration of the downtrodden. Elucidate.

themes.title: Widening of the national movement: ideological strands & global influences
themes.asks: Questions ask how the national movement widened its social base through new ideological strands in the 1920s (socialism, communism, peasant and worker movements), the new goals added (economic and social freedom), and world developments that motivated anti-colonial struggle.
checklist: Left wing: Nehru, Bose, CSP, communists, trade unions, Kisan Sabha
Purna Swaraj and the economic programme (Karachi resolution)
Global influences: Russian Revolution, World Wars, Irish and other anti-colonial movements
answer: Link each strand to the social group it brought in

questions.text: Since the decade of the 1920s, the national movement acquired various ideological strands and thereby expanded its social base. Discuss.
Highlight the importance of new objective that got added to the vision of Indian independence since the twenties of the last century.
What were the major political, economic and social developments in the world which motivated the anti- colonial struggle in India?

themes.title: Final phase: Quit India, Naval mutiny, Maulana Azad
themes.asks: UPSC asks about events leading to Quit India and its results, the naval mutiny's significance, and Maulana Azad's contributions.
checklist: Quit India: Cripps failure, war context, leaderless phase, parallel governments
RIN mutiny 1946 and why it signalled the end of British rule
Maulana Azad: Khilafat, Congress president, education minister, composite nationalism
answer: Cause → course → consequence structure

questions.text: What were the events that led to the Quit India Movement? Point out its results.
In what ways did the naval mutiny prove to be the last nail in the coffin of British colonial aspirations in India?
Discuss the contributions of Maulana Abul Kalam Azad to pre- and post-independent India.

themes.title: Historical underpinnings & making of the Constitution: Regulating Act 1773 to the Constituent Assembly
themes.asks: Questions ask how the Government of India Act 1935 helped the Constituent Assembly, and whether that Act laid down a federal constitution.
checklist: GoI Act 1935: federation, provincial autonomy, dyarchy at centre, federal court, lists
answer: Show specific provisions carried over
Link to Indian federalism's 'strong Centre' character

questions.text: Did the Government of India Act, 1935 lay down a federal constitution? Discuss.

It would have been difficult for the Constituent Assembly to complete its historic task of drafting the Constitution for Independent India in just three years but for the experience gained with the Government of India Act, 1935. Discuss.

ncert.book: NCERT Class 11 · Indian Constitution at Work

items.t: Regulating Act 1773: Governor-General of Bengal, Supreme Court at Calcutta
Pitt's India Act 1784: Board of Control, dual government
Charter Acts 1793, 1813 (trade monopoly ended except tea and China), 1833 (Governor-General of India), 1853
Government of India Act 1858: Crown takes over, Secretary of State
Indian Councils Acts 1861, 1892, 1909 (separate electorates)
Government of India Act 1919: dyarchy in provinces, bicameral centre
Simon Commission 1927 and the Nehru Report
Government of India Act 1935: All-India federation, provincial autonomy, dyarchy at centre, three lists, Federal Court
Cripps 1942 and Cabinet Mission 1946: how the Assembly was formed
Objectives Resolution, committees and the Drafting Committee (Ambedkar)
Adoption on 26 Nov 1949 (Constitution Day) and commencement on 26 Jan 1950
Indian Independence Act 1947 and dominion status
Sources of the Constitution: GoI Act 1935, UK, US, Ireland, Canada and others

themes.title: Integration & reorganisation of states: princely states, linguistic states, new & smaller states
themes.asks: A strong cross-paper theme. GS1 asks about princely state integration and linguistic reorganisation; GS2 asks whether smaller states mean better governance. Recent questions ask whether reorganisation came from popular pressure from below.
checklist: Integration of princely states: Patel, V.P. Menon, Junagadh, Hyderabad, Kashmir
Linguistic reorganisation: Potti Sriramulu, SRC 1953–56, effect on unity
New states: Uttarakhand, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Telangana — economic results
Arguments for and against smaller states
answer: Use both history and present governance evidence
End with a balanced view on unity and administrative efficiency

questions.text: Linguistic reorganization of Indian States was driven by popular pressure from below. Comment
The political and administrative reorganization of states and territories has been a continuous ongoing process since the mid-nineteenth century. Discuss with examples.
Assess the main administrative issues and socio-cultural problems in the integration process of Indian Princely States.
Discuss whether formation of new states in recent times is beneficial or not for the economy of India?
Has the formation of linguistic states strengthened the cause of Indian unity?

Many State Governments further bifurcate geographical administrative areas like Districts and Talukas for better governance. In light of the above, can it also be justified that more number of smaller States would bring in effective governance at State level? Discuss.

themes.title: Post-independence consolidation: polity, economy, Jai Jawan Jai Kisan
themes.asks: UPSC asks you to trace consolidation in the early years across polity, economy, education and foreign policy, and the meaning of slogans like 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'.
checklist: Polity: Constitution, first general election 1951–52, integration
Economy: planning, Industrial Policy 1948/1956, public sector
1965 war and food crisis behind 'Jai Jawan Jai Kisan'; Green Revolution push
answer: Use a dimension-wise structure (polity, economy, education, external)

questions.text: Trace India's consolidation process during early phase of independence in terms of polity, economy, education and international relations.
Write a critical note on the evolution and significance of the slogan, ‘Jai Jawan Jai Kisan’.

themes.title: Early foreign policy & wars: Tashkent, Bangladesh 1971, Gujral doctrine
themes.asks: Questions ask about the Tashkent Agreement, India's role in creating Bangladesh, and the Gujral doctrine's relevance today.
checklist: 1971: refugee crisis, security, Indo-Soviet treaty, outcome
Gujral doctrine principles and their echo in Neighbourhood First
answer: Link historical choices to present neighbourhood policy

questions.text: Analyze the circumstances that led to the Tashkent Agreement in 1966. Discuss the highlights of the Agreement.
Critically examine the compulsions which prompted India to play a decisive role in the emergence of Bangladesh.
What is meant by Gujral doctrine? Does it have any relevance today? Discuss.

themes.title: American & French Revolutions and their legacy
themes.asks: Questions ask about the American Revolution as an economic revolt against mercantilism and the French Revolution's continuing relevance.
checklist: Mercantilism and the colonies: Navigation Acts, Stamp Act, Townshend duties
Ideas: no taxation without representation, natural rights, Declaration of Independence
French Revolution: causes, Declaration of the Rights of Man, end of feudalism
Legacy: liberty, equality, fraternity in democracy, nationalism, human rights — including in India's Preamble
answer: For 'relevance today', match each revolutionary idea with a present institution or debate

questions.text: The French Revolution has enduring relevance to the contemporary world. Explain.
“American Revolution was an economic revolt against mercantilism.” Substantiate.

themes.title: Industrial Revolution and its spread: England, Japan, railways
themes.asks: UPSC asks why the Industrial Revolution began in England, life of workers then vs India today, Japan's 'latecomer' path, and the effects of railways worldwide.
checklist: Reasons for England's lead: capital, colonies, coal and iron, agricultural revolution, inventions
Social effects: urban slums, child labour, labour laws
Railways' socio-economic effects in different countries
answer: Comparisons work best as point-by-point contrasts

questions.text: Bring out the socio-economic effects of the introduction of railways in different countries of the world.
Why did the industrial revolution first occur in England? Discuss the quality of life of the people there during the industrialization. How does it compare with that in India at present?
“‘Latecomer’ Industrial Revolution in Japan involved certain factors that were markedly different from what West had experienced.” Analyze.

themes.title: World Wars, interwar crisis, Great Depression & ideologies
themes.asks: Questions ask whether WWI was about balance of power, Germany's responsibility for both wars, the threat to democracy between the wars, and policy responses to the Great Depression.
checklist: WWI causes: alliances, imperialism, nationalism, balance of power
Interwar: Versailles, rise of fascism and Nazism, failure of League
Great Depression: New Deal, Keynesian policies, protectionism
answer: Give a balanced verdict on 'how far' questions

questions.text: How far is it correct to say that the First World War was fought essentially for the preservation of balance of power?
“There arose a serious challenge to the Democratic State System between the two World Wars.” Evaluate the statement.
To what extent can Germany be held responsible for causing the two World Wars? Discuss critically
What policy instruments were deployed to contain the Great Economic Depression?

themes.title: Colonisation & decolonisation: Africa, Malaya, Suez
themes.asks: UPSC asks about decolonisation struggles in Africa and Malaya, the Suez crisis, and artificial African borders.
checklist: Scramble for Africa and Berlin Conference
Western-educated African elites leading anti-colonial movements
Suez 1956 and end of British power
answer: Use specific countries and leaders as examples

questions.text: What problems were germane to the decolonization process in the Malay Peninsula?
The anti-colonial struggles in West Africa were led by the new elite of Western educated Africans. Examine.
What were the events that led to the Suez Crisis in 1956? How did it deal a final blow to Britain’s self- image as a world power?
“Africa was chopped into States artificially created by accidents of European competition.” Analyze.

themes.title: Earth's interior, plate tectonics, mountains, islands & landforms
themes.asks: UPSC asks the mechanism behind landforms: continental drift, plate tectonics, mantle plumes, why fold mountains lie on continental margins, island arcs (Indonesia, Philippines), fjords, rocks, why India is a subcontinent, and how mountains affect weather.
checklist: Earth's interior and evidence (seismic waves, Juno-type missions)
Continental drift → sea-floor spreading → plate tectonics; mantle plume and hotspots
Fold mountains, island arcs, fjords, deltas
India as a subcontinent: physiography, Himalayan barrier
Mountain alignment and local weather (rain shadow, barrier effect)
answer: Draw a quick diagram (plate boundary, plume) — it saves words
Give world and Indian examples for each landform

questions.text: Discuss how the changes in shape and sizes of continents and ocean basins of the planet take place due to tectonic movements of the crustal masses.
How are the fjords formed? Why do they constitute some of the most picturesque areas of the world?
Describe the characteristics and type of primary rocks.
Why is India considered as a subcontinent? Elaborate your answer.
Briefly mention the alignment of major mountain ranges of the world and explain their impact on local weather conditions, with examples.
Define mantle plume and explain its role in plate tectonics.
How does the Juno Mission of NASA help to understand the origin and evolution of the Earth?
Why are the world’s fold mountain systems located along the margins of continents? Bring out the association between the global distribution of fold mountains and the earthquakes and volcanoes.
Explain the formation of thousands of islands in Indonesian and Philippines archipelagos.

(a) What do you understand by the theory of ‘continental drift’? Discuss t he prominent evidences in its support. (b) The recent cyclone on east coast of India was called ‘Phailin’. How are the tropical cyclones named across the world? Elaborate.

themes.title: Landslides in the Himalayas & Western Ghats
themes.asks: A cross-paper theme: GS1 asks why landslides are more frequent in the Himalayas than the Western Ghats; GS3 asks causes, effects and the National Landslide Risk Management Strategy.
checklist: Himalayas: young fold mountains, seismicity, rainfall, road-cutting, deforestation
Western Ghats: heavy rainfall, laterite soil, quarrying, plantations
NLRMS components: hazard mapping, early warning, awareness, mountain zone regulations
Mitigation: slope stabilisation, drainage, afforestation, building codes
answer: Comparison questions need a side-by-side of causes
End with a mitigation framework linked to NDMA

questions.text: Differentiate the causes of landslides in the Himalayan region and Western Ghats.
Describe the various causes and the effects of landslides. Mention the important components of the National Landslide Risk Management Strategy.
“The Himalayas are highly prone to landslides.” Discuss the causes and suggest suitable measures of mitigation.
(a) Bring out the causes for more frequent occurrence of landslides in the Himalayas than in the Western Ghats. (b) There is no formation of deltas by rivers of the Western Ghats. Why?

themes.title: Earthquakes, tsunamis & volcanoes: science to preparedness
themes.asks: GS1 asks how and where tsunamis, earthquakes and volcanoes occur (Circum-Pacific belt, 2021 eruptions); GS3 asks India's vulnerability, major quakes and preparedness gaps. Prepare the science and the management together.
checklist: Plate boundaries and Ring of Fire; volcano types and effects
India's seismic zones; major quakes (Latur, Bhuj, Kashmir, Sikkim, Nepal 2015)
Preparedness: NDMA guidelines, building codes, early warning (INCOIS), drills
answer: Start with the mechanism, then impact, then preparedness — this sequence answers both GS1 and GS3 versions

questions.text: What are Tsunamis? How and where are they formed? What are their consequences? Explain with examples.
Mention the global occurrence of volcanic eruptions in 2021 and their impact on regional environment.

Discuss about the vulnerability of India to earthquake related hazards. Give examples including the salient features of major disasters caused by earthquakes in different parts of India during the last three decades.
Discuss the geophysical characteristics of Circum-Pacific Zone.

On December 2004, tsunami brought havoc on fourteen countries including India. Discuss the factors responsible for occurrence of tsunami and its effects on life and economy. In the light of guidelines of NDMA (2010) describe the mechanisms for preparedness to reduce the risk during such events.
The frequency of earthquakes appears to have increased in the Indian subcontinent. However, India’s preparedness for mitigating their impact has significant gaps. Discuss various aspects.

themes.title: Atmosphere, air masses, winds, inversion, deserts & auroras
themes.asks: Questions ask about atmospheric processes: troposphere's role, air masses, temperature inversion, urban heat islands, location of hot deserts, local winds (Loo, Chinook, Foehn), and auroras.
checklist: Atmospheric layers and why weather happens in the troposphere
Trade winds and desert location on western margins
answer: Diagrams help; always add an Indian or world example

questions.text: Compare the Loo, Chinook and Foehn winds with respect to their regions of prevalence, their nature and climatic impacts
What are aurora australis and aurora borealis? How are these triggered?
Troposphere is a very significant atmosphere layer that determines weather processes. How?
Discuss the concept of air mass and explain its role in macro-climatic changes.

(a) Bring out the causes for the formation of heat islands in the urban habitat of the world. (b) What do you understand by the phenomenon of ‘temperature inversion’ in meteorology? How does it affect weather and the habitants of the place?
Major hot deserts in northern hemisphere are located between 20-30 deg N latitudes and on the western side of the continents. Why?

themes.title: Monsoon, El Niño & drought
themes.asks: UPSC asks about monsoon mechanism and culture, monsoon Asia feeding half the world, changing monsoon due to human landscapes, El Niño's effects, and drought preparedness.
checklist: Monsoon mechanism: differential heating, ITCZ, jet streams, Tibetan plateau
El Niño, La Niña, IOD and Indian rainfall
Human-induced changes: land use, aerosols, urbanisation
Drought as disaster: NDMA guidelines, monitoring, contingency crop plans
Monsoon and culture (e.g. Purvaiya in Bhojpur)
answer: Link the physical process to agriculture and food security in your conclusion

questions.text: Why is the South-West Monsoon called Purvaiys’ (easterly) in Bhojpur Region? How has this directional seasonal wind systems influenced the cultural ethos of the region?
What characteristics can be assigned to monsoon climate that succeeds in feeding more than 50 percent of the world population residing in Monsoon Asia?
How far do you agree that the behaviour of the Indian monsoon has been changing due to humanizing landscapes? Discuss.
Most of the unusual climatic happenings are explained as an outcome of the El-Nino effect. Do you agree?

Drought has been recognized as a disaster in view of its spatial expanse, temporal duration, slow onset and lasting effects on vulnerable sections. With a focus on the September 2010 guidelines from the National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), discuss the mechanisms for preparedness to deal with likely El Niño and La Niña fallouts in India.

themes.title: Tropical cyclones, twisters & cyclone warnings
themes.asks: Questions repeat on cyclone formation and location (SST rise, Fujiwhara effect, Bay of Bengal vs Arabian Sea), twisters in the Gulf of Mexico, and IMD colour-coded warnings.
checklist: Conditions for tropical cyclones: SST above 26–27°C, Coriolis, low wind shear
Why Bay of Bengal, South China Sea, Gulf of Mexico
answer: Use a diagram of a cyclone's structure; end with preparedness

questions.text: What is the Fujiwhara effect? Explain its impact on the movement and intensity of tropical cyclones
What is sea surface temperature rise? How does it affect the formation of tropical cyclones?
What is a twister? Why are the majority of twisters observed in areas around the Gulf of Mexico?
Discuss the meaning of colour-coded weather warnings for cyclone prone areas given by India Meteorological Department.
Tropical cyclones are largely confined to South China Sea, Bay of Bengal and Gulf of Mexico. Why?

themes.title: Cloudbursts & extreme rainfall
themes.asks: GS1 and GS3 both ask the mechanism of cloudbursts, recent examples, and NDMA measures for the Himalayas (Uttarakhand).
checklist: Mechanism: orographic lifting, moisture convergence, sudden release
Examples: Kedarnath 2013, Himachal and Uttarakhand events
Mitigation: Doppler radar, early warning, land-use zoning, river-bank regulation
answer: Mechanism → recent example → NDMA-based measures

questions.text: What is the phenomenon of 'cloudbursts'? Explain.
Explain the mechanism and occurrence of cloudburst in the context of Indian subcontinent. Discuss two recent examples.
With reference to National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines, discuss the measures to be adopted to mitigate the impact of recent incidents of cloudbursts in many places of Uttarakhand.

themes.title: Oceans & marine environment: currents, salinity, dead zones, oil pollution, marine resources
themes.asks: UPSC asks about forces behind ocean currents and their role in climate, fishing and navigation; salinity variations; dead zones; oil pollution; and ocean resources for the resource crisis.
checklist: Currents: wind, Coriolis, temperature, salinity; warm vs cold currents
Fishing grounds where warm and cold currents meet
Oil spills: impacts on marine life and coasts
Ocean resources: minerals, energy, food, deep sea mission
answer: Map-based examples (Grand Banks, Peru) add marks

questions.text: What is oil pollution? What are its impacts on the marine ecosystem? In what way is pollution particularly harmful for a country like India.
What are the forces that influence ocean currents? Describe their role in the fishing industry of the world.
What are the consequences of spreading of ‘Dead Zones’ on marine ecosystems?
Account for variations in oceanic salinity and discuss its multidimensional effects.
Explain the factors responsible for the origin of ocean currents? How do they influence regional climates, fishing and navigation?
Critically evaluate the various resources of the oceans which can be harnessed to meet the resource crisis in the world.

themes.title: Coastal zone: resources, erosion & hazard preparedness
themes.asks: Questions ask about the resource potential of India's coastline, hazard preparedness, and coastal erosion with management techniques.
checklist: Coastal resources: ports, fisheries, minerals, tourism, blue economy
Hazards: cyclones, tsunami, sea-level rise, erosion
Causes of erosion: natural and human (ports, sand mining)
Hard and soft engineering: seawalls, groynes, mangroves, beach nourishment
answer: Pair each hazard with a management response

questions.text: Comment on the resource potentials of the long coastline of India and highlight the status of natural hazard preparedness in these areas.
Explain the causes and effects of coastal erosion in India. What are the available coastal management techniques for combating the hazard?

themes.title: Minerals & mining: resource vs environment
themes.asks: Cross-paper: GS1 asks about mineral distribution (Gondwana, Deccan trap) and why mining's GDP share is low; GS3 asks why mining is an environmental hazard, illegal mining and go/no-go zones.
checklist: Gondwana coal, Dharwar metallic minerals, Deccan trap resources
Low GDP share: regulation, exploration gaps, technology, land issues
Environmental impacts: deforestation, water, air, displacement
Illegal mining, go/no-go zones, MMDR reforms, District Mineral Foundation
answer: Balance development needs with environmental costs
Use specific mining regions as examples

questions.text: Mineral resources are fundamental to the country's economy and these are exploited by mining. Why is mining considered an environmental hazard? Explain the remedial measures required to reduce the environmental hazard due to mining.
Discuss the natural resource potential of ‘Deccan trap’.
Despite India being one of the countries of Gondwanaland, its mining industry contributes much less to its Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in percentage. Discuss.
“In spite of adverse environmental impact, coal mining is still inevitable for development”. Discuss.
What are the consequences of Illegal mining? Discuss the Ministry of Environment and Forests’ concept of GO AND NO GO zones for coal mining sector.

themes.title: Oil & gas: global distribution, shale, refineries
themes.asks: UPSC asks about world distribution of oil (on-shore vs off-shore), multi-dimensional impacts of uneven distribution, shale gas in India, and why refineries are located away from oil fields.
checklist: Sedimentary basins and off-shore continental shelves
Shale gas: reserves, water and technology constraints
answer: Connect geography to economic and geopolitical consequences

questions.text: Give a geographical explanation of the distribution of off-shore oil reserves of the world. How are they different from the on-shore occurrences of oil reserves?
Discuss the multi-dimensional implications of uneven distribution of mineral oil in the world.
Petroleum refineries are not necessarily located nearer to crude oil producing areas, particularly in many of the developing countries. Explain its implications.

It is said that India has substantial reserves of shale oil and gas, which can feed the needs of the country for quarter century. However, tapping of the resource does not appear to be high on the agenda. Discuss critically the availability and issues involved.

themes.title: Polar regions: Arctic resources, tundra & India's interest
themes.asks: Questions ask why India is interested in the Arctic, the economic and environmental impacts of Arctic oil, and tundra's fragility.
checklist: Arctic: new sea routes, resources, climate science, India's Arctic Policy, Himadri station
answer: Balance economic gain against ecological risk

questions.text: Tundra regions are ecologically fragile but economically important. Examine this statement critically
Why is India taking keen interest in resources of Arctic region?
What are the economic significances of discovery of oil in Arctic Sea and its possible environmental consequences?

themes.title: Glaciers, cryosphere & sea-level rise
themes.asks: A heavily repeated theme: melting Himalayan glaciers and water resources, Arctic vs Antarctic melting effects, cryosphere and global climate, sea-level rise threatening island nations, and IPCC projections for India.
checklist: Himalayan glacier retreat and river flows
Arctic sea ice vs Antarctic land ice: different effects
Sea-level rise: small island states, Indian coasts, Indian Ocean region
answer: Link physical change → human impact → adaptation

questions.text: How are climate change and the sea level rise affecting the very existence of many island nations? Discuss with examples.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has predicted a global sea level rise of about one metre by AD 2100. What would be its impact in India and the other countries in the Indian Ocean region?
How do the melting of the Arctic ice and glaciers of the Antarctic differently affect the weather patterns and human activities on the Earth? Explain.
How will the melting of Himalayan glaciers have a far-reaching impact on the water resources of India?
How does the cryosphere affect global climate?
Bring out the relationship between the shrinking Himalayan glaciers and the symptoms of climate change in the Indian sub-continent.

themes.title: Location of industries: steel, refineries, sugar, textiles, tea, rubber, corridors
themes.asks: UPSC asks location factors for specific industries: iron and steel away from raw material, refineries, sugar shifting south, decentralised cotton textiles, tea gardens limited to Darjeeling, rubber, industrial corridors, and non-farm primary activities.
checklist: Weber-type factors: raw material, market, transport, labour, power, policy
Iron and steel: shift to coastal and market locations
Sugar: southern advantage (yield, crushing season, cooperatives)
Cotton textiles: decentralised due to market and power
answer: Always give specific locations; a rough map sketch helps

questions.text: What are non-farm primary activities? How are these activities related to physiographic features in India? Discuss with suitable examples.
Describing the distribution of rubber-producing countries indicate the major environmental issues faced by them.
Account for the present location of iron and steel industries away from the source of raw material, by giving examples.
What is the significance of Industrial Corridors in India? Identifying industrial corridors, explain their main characteristics.
Whereas the British planters had developed tea gardens all along the Shivaliks and Lesser Himalayas from Assam to Himachal Pradesh, in effect they did not succeed beyond the Darjeeling area. Explain.
Account for the change in the spatial pattern of the Iron and Steel industry in the world.

(a) Do you agree that there is a growing trend of opening new sugar mills in southern States of India? Discuss with justification. (b) Analyze the factors for the highly decentralized cotton textile industry in India.

themes.title: Desertification, land degradation & land-use change
themes.asks: Questions ask about desertification across climate zones, aeolian processes, drivers of land-use change, and reclamation of water bodies for urban use.
checklist: Desertification causes: overgrazing, deforestation, salinity, climate
Land-use change drivers: urbanisation, agriculture, mining
Reclamation of wetlands for urban use and its effects (floods, heat)
answer: Use examples beyond deserts to show desertification has no climate boundary

questions.text: Discuss the role of aeolian processes in desertification and land degradation
Analyze the major drivers of human-induced land-use changes in India and their geographical consequences
What are the environmental implications of the reclamation of the water bodies into urban land use? Explain with examples.
The process of desertification does not have climate boundaries. Justify with examples.

themes.title: Forests, natural vegetation & biodiversity
themes.asks: UPSC asks about diversity of natural vegetation, forest status and climate change, biodiversity variation, the Biological Diversity Act, and the Kunming–Montreal framework.
checklist: Forest cover status (ISFR) and carbon sinks
Biological Diversity Act 2002: NBA, SBB, BMCs, access and benefit sharing
answer: Use data points carefully; name protected areas

questions.text: Discuss the aim and goals of Kunming-Montreal global biodiversity framework. Mention India’s commitments and initiatives to achieve the goals and targets of this framework giving suitable examples.
Identify and discuss the factors responsible for diversity of natural vegetation in India Assess the significance of wildlife sanctuaries in rain forest regions of India.
Examine the status of forest resources of India and its resultant impact on climate change.
How does biodiversity vary in India? How is the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 helpful in conservation of flora and fauna?

themes.title: Wetlands & Ramsar sites
themes.asks: Questions ask about the Ramsar concept of 'wise use', the National Wetland Conservation Programme and examples of Ramsar sites.
answer: Name at least two or three Ramsar sites

questions.text: Comment on the National Wetland Conservation Programme initiated by the Government of India and name a few India’s wetlands of international importance included in the Ramsar Sites.
What is wetland? Explain the Ramsar concept of ‘wise use’ in the context of wetland conservation. Cite two examples of Ramsar sites from India.

themes.title: Fragile Himalayan ecosystems: tourism & infrastructure
themes.asks: UPSC asks whether Himalayan states have crossed their carrying capacity due to tourism, and how to balance infrastructure with disaster risk in ecologically sensitive areas.
checklist: Carrying capacity concept; tourism pressure (J&K, Himachal, Uttarakhand)
Joshimath, Char Dham road, hydropower debates
answer: Give balanced arguments and concrete safeguards

questions.text: Discuss how the contradiction between ‘rapid infrastructure development’ and ‘disaster-risk reduction’ in ecologically-sensitive areas of India can be managed, with suitable examples.
The states of Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand are reaching the limits of their ecological carrying capacity due to tourism. Critically evaluate.

themes.title: Water security: scarcity, conservation & management
themes.asks: A cross-paper favourite: freshwater crisis, why India suffers scarcity despite endowment, managing land and water, urban water harvesting, micro-watersheds, Jal Shakti Abhiyan, and new water technologies.
checklist: Supply vs access vs quality problems
Causes of scarcity: uneven distribution, wastage, pollution, groundwater overuse
Rainwater harvesting, micro-watershed development, Jal Shakti Abhiyan, Atal Bhujal
Alternative technologies: desalination, atmospheric water, wastewater reuse
answer: Structure: problem → causes → measures (supply side, demand side, governance)

questions.text: The world is facing an acute shortage of clean and safe freshwater. What are the alternative technologies which can solve this crisis? Briefly discuss any three such technologies citing their key merits and demerits.
Why is the world today enfronted with a crisis of availability of and access to freshwater resources?
What are the salient features of the Jal Shakti Abhiyan launched by the Government of India for water conservation and water security?
“The ideal solution of depleting ground water resources in India is water harvesting system”. How can it be made effective in urban areas?
The effective management of land and water resources will drastically reduce the human miseries. Explain.
In what way micro-watershed development projects help in water conservation in drought-prone and semi-arid regions of India?
India is well endowed with fresh water resources. Critically examine why it still suffers from water scarcity.

themes.title: Groundwater depletion & seawater intrusion
themes.asks: Questions ask about groundwater decline in the Gangetic plain and its effect on food security, causes of depletion, government steps, and seawater intrusion in coastal aquifers.
checklist: Causes: free power, water-intensive crops, tube wells
Atal Bhujal Yojana, CGWA rules, recharge
answer: Always link depletion to cropping patterns and power subsidies

questions.text: Examine the factors responsible for depleting groundwater in India. What are the steps taken by the government to mitigate such depletion?
Seawater intrusion in the coastal aquifers is a major concern in India. What are the causes of seawater intrusion and the remedial measures to combat this hazard?
The groundwater potential of the gangetic valley is on a serious decline. How may it affect the food security of India?

themes.title: Irrigation & water-use efficiency
themes.asks: UPSC asks about challenges in irrigation, water-use efficiency, micro-irrigation, storage, and turning floods into irrigation and navigation.
checklist: Irrigation types and issues: inefficiency, silting, unequal access
Micro-irrigation: drip, sprinkler, PMKSY 'Per Drop More Crop'
answer: Use data on water-use efficiency where you can

questions.text: What are the major challenges faced by Indian irrigation system in recent times? State the measures taken by the government for efficient irrigation management.
How and to what extent would micro-irrigation help in solving India’s water crisis?
Suggest measures to improve water storage and irrigation system to make its judicious use under depleting scenario.
In what way can floods be converted into a sustainable source of irrigation and all-weather inland navigation in India?
What is water-use efficiency? Describe the role of micro-irrigation in increasing the water-use efficiency.

themes.title: River interlinking & water disputes: inter-state and transboundary
themes.asks: A cross-paper theme linking geography, federalism and foreign policy: river interlinking pros and cons, inter-state water disputes, Indus Water Treaty, and water conflict in South Asia.
checklist: River interlinking: Ken-Betwa, benefits, environmental and displacement costs
Inter-state disputes: Art 262, tribunals, Cauvery, delays
Indus Water Treaty and its implications
Transboundary rivers: Teesta, Brahmaputra, Ganga treaty
answer: Pull in federalism (GS2) and IR (GS2) angles even when the question is from GS1

questions.text: Water resources are both an asset and a source of conflict in South Asia. Examine this statement giving examples
The interlinking of rivers can provide viable solutions to the multi-dimensional inter-related problems of droughts, floods, and interrupted navigation. Critically examine.
Not many years ago, river linking was a concept but it is becoming reality in the country. Discuss the advantages of river linking and its possible impact on the environment.
Present an account of the Indus Water Treaty and examine its ecological, economic and political implications in the context of changing bilateral relations.
Constitutional mechanisms to resolve the inter-state water disputes have failed to address and solve the problems. Is the failure due to structural or process inadequacy or both? Discuss.

themes.title: Diversity & national unity
themes.asks: UPSC asks about unity in diversity, whether regions form cultural units more than states, tolerance as a feature of Indian society, cultural elements of diversity, and links between diversity and marginality.
checklist: Forms of diversity: language, religion, caste, region, ethnicity
Bonds of unity: geography, culture, constitution, economy
answer: Use examples from different regions; avoid generic statements

questions.text: Unity in diversity remains the defining feature of Indian society despite the challenges from communalism and regionalism. Comment
Critically analyse the proposition that there is a high correlation between India's cultural diversities and socio-economic marginalities.
In the context of the diversity of India, can it be said that the regions form cultural units rather than the States? Give reasons with examples for your viewpoint.
The spirit of tolerance and love is not only an interesting feature of Indian society from very early times, but it is also playing an important part at the present. Elaborate.
Describe any four cultural elements of diversity in India and rate their relative significance in building a national identity.

themes.title: Family, marriage, traditions & social values
themes.asks: Questions ask whether marriage as a sacrament is losing value, how society maintains continuity of values, whether customs suppress reason, and whether joint families depend on economic factors.
checklist: Marriage: sacrament vs contract, changes due to education and urbanisation
Joint to nuclear family and its causes
Continuity and change in traditional values
answer: Use sociological terms and present examples

questions.text: Do you think marriage as a sacrament is loosing its value in Modern India?
How does Indian society maintain continuity in traditional social values? Enumerate the changes taking place in it.
Customs and traditions suppress reason leading to obscurantism. Do you agree?
The life cycle of a joint family depends on economic factors rather than social values. Discuss.

themes.title: Caste: continuity, change, mobility & Dalit assertion
themes.asks: A heavily repeated GS1 theme: is caste disappearing in urban India, fluid and static identity, new associational forms, Dalit assertion, and intercaste vs interreligious marriages.
checklist: Caste in urban vs rural India
Fluid vs static: mobility vs endogamy
Dalit movements and annihilation of caste
answer: Use sociological concepts (Srinivas etc.) and current examples
Balance continuity and change

questions.text: Is caste disappearing in urban India? Illustrate your answer with examples
Intercaste marriages between castes which have socio-economic parity have increased, to some extent, but this is less true of interreligious marriages. Discuss.
Why is caste identity in India both fluid and static?
Has caste lost its relevance in understanding the multi-cultural Indian Society? Elaborate your answer with illustrations.
“Caste system is assuming new identities and associational forms. Hence caste system cannot be eradicated in India.” Comment.
Debate the issue of whether and how contemporary movements for assertion of Dalit identity work towards annihilation of caste.

themes.title: Tribal identity, rights & development
themes.asks: UPSC asks about tribal diversity vs single category, tribal knowledge systems, why 'Scheduled Tribes', constitutional provisions, legal initiatives against discrimination, and whether development centres on displacement and rehabilitation.
checklist: Constitutional provisions: Fifth and Sixth Schedules, Art 342, 244, 275
answer: Combine sociology (GS1) with policy (GS2) and security (GS3) angles

questions.text: Does India’s tribal development policy reflect the aspirations for a socially grounded and equity-based governance? Justify your answer
Does tribal development in India centre around two axes, those of displacement and of rehabilitation? Give your opinion.
Given the diversities among tribal communities in India in which specific context should they be considered as a single category?
Examine the uniqueness of tribal knowledge systems when compared with mainstream knowledge and cultural systems.
What are the two major legal initiatives by the State since Independence addressing discrimination against Scheduled Tribes (STs)?
Why are the tribals in India referred to as ‘the Scheduled Tribes’? Indicate the major provisions enshrined in the Constitution of India for their upliftment.

themes.title: Population & demographic transition
themes.asks: Questions ask about demographic transition, demographic winter, population and poverty, population education, and population density in the Ganga basin.
checklist: Demographic transition stages and India's position
Density and resources in the Ganga basin
answer: Use data (TFR, dependency ratio) carefully

questions.text: Critically examine the challenges of demographic transition in contemporary India
Discuss the distribution and density of population in the Ganga River Basin with special reference to land, soil and water resources.
What is the concept of a 'demographic winter'? Is the world moving towards such a situation? Elaborate.
Discuss the main objectives of Population Education and point out the measures to achieve them in India in detail.
Critically examine whether growing population is the cause of poverty OR poverty is the main cause of population increase in India.

themes.title: Ageing population & elderly care
themes.asks: UPSC asks about the effect of globalisation on the aged, newer health challenges due to rising life expectancy, and geriatric health care.
checklist: Health challenges: NCDs, dementia, care gaps
Schemes and laws: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents Act, NPHCE
answer: Link social change (GS1) to health policy (GS2)

questions.text: The increase in life expectancy in the country has led to newer health challenges in the community. What are those challenges and what steps need to be taken to meet them?
In order to enhance the prospects of social development, sound and adequate health care policies are needed particularly in the fields of geriatric and maternal health care. Discuss.
Critically examine the effect of globalization on the aged population in India.

themes.title: Migration: internal, international & illegal
themes.asks: Questions ask why big cities attract more migrants, changing labour migration trends, and illegal cross-border migration as a security threat.
checklist: Push and pull factors; rural-urban migration
Labour migration within and outside India (Gulf)
Illegal migration from neighbours: security, demographic effects, border fencing
answer: Combine society and security angles

questions.text: Why do large cities tend to attract more migrants than smaller towns? Discuss in the light of conditions in developing countries.
Discuss the changes in the trends of labour migration within and outside India in the last four decades.
How does illegal transborder migration pose a threat to India’s security? Discuss the strategies to curb this, bringing out the factors which give impetus to such migration.

themes.title: Urbanisation: social problems, segregation & urban poverty
themes.asks: UPSC asks about social problems of rapid urbanisation, segregation and marginalisation of the poor, and whether smart cities address urban poverty.
answer: Use specific cities and data

questions.text: How does smart city in India, address the issues of urban poverty and distributive justice?
Does urbanisation lead to more segregation and/or marginalization of the poor in Indian metropolises?
Discuss the various social problems which originated out of the speedy process of urbanization in India.

themes.title: New urban economy: IT hubs, tier-2 cities & new middle class
themes.asks: Questions ask about IT hubs' new employment and new problems, the socio-economic effects of IT industries in big cities, and tier-2 cities with a consumption-oriented new middle class.
checklist: IT hubs: Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune — jobs, migration, real estate
Problems: inequality, traffic, water stress, cost of living, gated enclaves
Tier-2 cities: new middle class, malls, aspiration, consumption culture
answer: Balance opportunities and problems with named cities

questions.text: How is the growth of Tier 2 cities related to the rise of a new middle class with an emphasis on the culture of consumption?
What are the main socio-economic implications arising out of the development of IT industries in major cities of India?
“The growth of cities as I.T. hubs has opened up new avenues of employment, but has also created new problems”. Substantiate this statement with examples.

themes.title: Smart cities, rural–urban integration & urban transport
themes.asks: UPSC asks about Smart Cities Mission objectives, smart villages, rural-urban integration (PURA, RURBAN), and urban transport.
checklist: Smart Cities Mission: area-based development, pan-city solutions
PURA and Shyama Prasad Mukherji RURBAN Mission
answer: Link to urban local governance (74th Amendment)

questions.text: With a brief background of quality of urban life in India, introduce the objectives and strategy of the ‘Smart City Programme.’

What are ‘Smart Cities’? Examine their relevance for urban development in India. Will it increase rural- urban differences? Give arguments for ’Smart Villages’ in the light of PURA and RURBAN Mission.
Smart cities in India cannot sustain without smart villages. Discuss this statement in the backdrop of rural urban integration.
The basis of providing urban amenities in rural areas (PURA) is rooted in establishing connectivity. Comment.

themes.title: Urban floods
themes.asks: Cross-paper and frequent: why big cities (including smart ones) flood, causes, major floods (Mumbai, Chennai), and policies to tackle them.
checklist: Causes: encroachment of water bodies, poor drainage, concretisation, extreme rainfall
Major floods: Mumbai 2005, Chennai 2015, Hyderabad, Pune
NDMA urban flood guidelines, sponge cities, early warning
answer: Name two floods with features; end with a framework of measures

questions.text: Flooding in urban areas is an emerging climate-induced disaster. Discuss the causes of this disaster. Mention the features of two such major floods in the last two decades in India. Describe the policies and frameworks in India that aim at tackling such floods.
Account for the huge flooding of million cities in India including the smart ones like Hyderabad and Pune. Suggest lasting remedial measures.
Major cities of India are becoming vulnerable to flood conditions. Discuss.

The frequency of urban floods due to high intensity rainfall is increasing over the years. Discussing the reasons for urban floods, highlight the mechanisms for preparedness to reduce the risk during such events.

themes.title: Globalisation & Indian society and culture
themes.asks: UPSC repeatedly asks how globalisation affects Indian society: consumer culture, cultural diversity, homogenisation vs specificity, youth, and the elderly.
checklist: Positive and negative effects of globalisation on culture
Effect on youth, women, elderly, family
answer: Avoid one-sided answers; UPSC expects balance

questions.text: Evaluate the impact of globalization on Indian youths with reference to social, political, economic and cultural spheres
Do you think that globalization results in only an aggressive consumer culture? Justify your answer.
Is diversity and pluralism in India under threat due to globalization? Justify your answer.
‘Globalization is generally said to promote cultural homogenization but due to this cultural specificities appear to be strengthened in the Indian Society.’ Elucidate.
To what extent globalisation has influenced the core of cultural diversity in India? Explain.

themes.title: Technology & social change: mobiles, WFH, fast food, crypto, digital education
themes.asks: Questions ask about technology's social effects: mobiles replacing child-parent bonding, work from home on families, fast food, cryptocurrency, digital education, and digital tech for empowerment.
checklist: Crypto: what it is and social effects
answer: Give both sides with Indian examples

questions.text: Do you think digital technology promotes social empowerment? Explain with examples
How do you account for the growing fast food industries given that there are increased health concerns in modern society? Illustrate your answer with the Indian experience.
Child cuddling is now being replaced by mobile phones. Discuss its impact on the socialization of children.
Explore and evaluate the impact of ‘Work From Home’ on family relationships.
Elucidate the relationship between globalization and new technology in a world of scarce resources with special reference to India.
What is Cryptocurrency? How does it affect global society? Has it been affecting Indian society also?
How have digital initiatives in India contributed to the functioning of the education system in the country? Elaborate your answer.

themes.title: Secularism: Indian vs Western models
themes.asks: Cross-paper: GS1 asks how Indian secularism differs from Western models; GS2 compares with the US and France. Prepare one comparative frame for both.
checklist: Indian secularism: principled distance, equal respect, state intervention in religion
Western/US: wall of separation; France: laïcité
answer: A comparison table (India vs US vs France) answers both papers

questions.text: Discuss India as a secular state and compare with the secular principles of the US constitution.
Are tolerance, assimilation and pluralism the key elements in the making of an Indian form of secularism? Justify your answer.
What can France learn from the Indian Constitution’s approach to secularism?
How the Indian concept of secularism is different from the western model of secularism? Discuss.
How do the Indian debates on secularism differ from the debates in the West?

themes.title: Communalism, sect & radicalisation
themes.asks: Questions ask about causes of communalism (power struggle, relative deprivation), religiosity turning into communalism, sect's salience, post-liberal identity politics, and radicalism from the neighbourhood.
checklist: Radicalisation and its internal security link
answer: Use examples carefully and neutrally

questions.text: Discuss the impact of post-liberal economy on ethnic identity and communalism.
Analyse the salience of ‘sect’ in Indian society vis-a-vis caste, region and religion.
‘Communalism arises either due to power struggle or relative deprivation’. Argue by giving suitable illustrations.
Distinguish between religiousness/religiosity and communalism giving one example of how the former has got transformed into the latter in independent India.

“The diverse nature of India as a multi-religious and multi-ethnic society is not immune to the impact of radicalism which is seen in her neighbourhood.” Discuss along with strategies to be adopted to counter this environment.

themes.title: Regionalism & regional disparity
themes.asks: UPSC asks the basis of regionalism, whether it stems from cultural assertion or unequal development, regional disparity vs diversity, and demands for separate states.
answer: Separate regionalism (identity) from regional disparity (development)

questions.text: What is regional disparity? How does it differ from diversity? How serious is the issue of regional disparity in India?
Do you agree that regionalism in India appears to be a consequence of rising cultural assertiveness? Argue
What is the basis of regionalism? Is it that unequal distribution of benefits of development on regional basis eventually promotes regionalism? Substantiate your answer.

“If amendment bill to the Whistleblowers Protection Act, 2011 tabled in the Parliament is passed, there may be no one left to protect.” Critically evaluate.
‘A national Lokpal, however strong it may be, cannot resolve the problems of immorality in public affairs.’ Discuss.

themes.title: Citizens' Charter & citizen-centric administration

Right to Services Acts in states
answer: Problem-solution format; cite 2nd ARC and Sevottam

Though Citizens’ charters have been formulated by many public service delivery organizations, there is no corresponding improvement in the level of citizens’ satisfaction and quality of services being provided. Analyse.

themes.title: E-governance & the digital divide

checklist: E-governance models: broadcasting, critical flow, comparative analysis, mobilisation, interactive service
Digital India pillars; examples (UMANG, DigiLocker, CPGRAMS, e-Courts, GeM)
Digital divide: rural access, literacy, language, gender
Data protection and cyber risks in e-governance
answer: Name the model asked and give one Indian example for each point
End with inclusion: assisted access (CSCs), vernacular interfaces

questions.text: E-governance projects have a built-in bias towards technology and back-end integration than user-centric designs. Examine.

Has digital illiteracy, particularly in rural areas, coupled with lack of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) accessibility hindered socio-economic development? Examine with justification.
“The emergence of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (Digital Revolution) has initiated e-Governance as an integral part of government”. Discuss.
E-governance is not only about utilization of the power of new technology, but also much about critical importance of the ‘use value’ of information. Explain.

themes.title: DBT, Aadhaar & digital welfare delivery
themes.asks: Cross-paper GS2–GS3: DBT as a progressive but limited reform, electronic cash transfers to cut corruption, Aadhaar vs NPR, and how DBT changes the subsidy scenario.

Price subsidy vs DBT: fertiliser, LPG (PAHAL), food
answer: Present benefits and limits with data
Link to GS3 subsidy reform

In what way could replacement of price subsidy with Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) change the scenario of subsidies in India? Discuss.

On merits, discuss whether or not both schemes need run concurrently. Analyse the potential of the schemes to achieve developmental benefits and equitable growth.
Electronic cash transfer system for the welfare schemes is an ambitious project to minimize corruption, eliminate wastage and facilitate reforms. Comment.

themes.title: Civil services in a democracy: ethos, neutrality, reforms

checklist: Role of civil services in democracy; Patel's 'steel frame'
Generalist vs specialist debate; lateral entry
Mission Karmayogi, performance appraisal, tenure (TSR Subramanian case)
answer: Use committees and judgments as evidence
Tie to GS4 values where it fits

questions.text: Analyse the advantages and limitations of the generalist structure of the Indian Civil Services in contemporary governance
The ethos of civil service in India stand for the combination of professionalism with nationalistic consciousness – Elucidate.
The Doctrine of Democratic Governance makes it necessary that the public perception of the integrity and commitment of civil servants becomes absolutely positive. Discuss.
“Institutional quality is a crucial driver of economic performance”. In this context suggest reforms in the Civil Service for strengthening democracy.

Initially Civil Services in India were designed to achieve the goals of neutrality and effectiveness, which seems to be lacking in the present context. Do you agree with the view that drastic reforms are required in Civil Services. Comment.
“Traditional bureaucratic structure and culture have hampered the process of socio-economic development in India.” Comment.
Has the Cadre based Civil Services Organization been the cause of slow change in India? Critically examine.

themes.title: Public health system & universal health coverage

Public health spending vs out-of-pocket expenditure
Public vs private: regulation, PPP, strategic purchasing
answer: Use NFHS/NHA data
Structure: gaps → state's role → private role → reforms

questions.text: In a crucial domain like the public healthcare system the Indian State should play a vital role to contain the adverse impact of marketisation of the system. Suggest some measures through which the State can enhance the reach of public healthcare at the grassroots level.
“Besides being a moral imperative of a Welfare State, primary health structure is a necessary precondition for sustainable development.” Analyse.
Appropriate local community-level healthcare intervention is a prerequisite to achieve ‘Health for All’ in India. Explain.
Public health system has limitations in providing universal health coverage. Do you think that private sector could help in bridging the gap? What other viable alternatives would you suggest?
Identify the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) that are related to health. Discuss the success of the actions taken by the Government for achieving the same.

themes.title: Pandemics & global health: COVID-19, WHO, vaccines
themes.asks: UPSC asks about WHO's performance in COVID-19, how vaccines work and the platforms Indian manufacturers used, and technology for pandemic management.
checklist: WHO: IHR, delays, funding dependence, pandemic treaty
Vaccine principle: antigen and immune memory; platforms (inactivated, viral vector, mRNA, DNA)
Indian vaccines: Covaxin, Covishield, ZyCoV-D; Vaccine Maitri
Technology: CoWIN, Aarogya Setu, genome sequencing (INSACOG), telemedicine (eSanjeevani)

questions.text: What is the basic principle behind vaccine development? How do vaccines work? What approaches were adopted by the Indian vaccine manufacturers to produce COVID-19 vaccines?
Critically examine the role of WHO in providing global health security during the Covid-19 pandemic.

COVID-19 pandemic has caused unprecedented devastation worldwide. However, technological advancements are being availed readily to win over the crisis. Give an account of how technology was sought to aid management of the pandemic.

themes.title: Education policy: NEP, RTE, higher education, exams
themes.asks: Questions ask welfare obligation vs strategic investment, aims of the Public Examinations Act 2024, RTE's inadequacy, NEP 2020 and SDG-4, Amartya Sen's reforms in primary education and health, foreign universities, and autonomy of IITs and IIMs.
checklist: NEP 2020: 5+3+3+4, foundational literacy, multidisciplinary higher education, HECI
